```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg", dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_cc <- requireNamespace("CoordinateCleaner", quietly = TRUE)
```

Eight of the tests compare a record with reference data from a shipped layer: points (capitals, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions, artificial hotspots) and polygons (land, urban areas, countries). The ninth, `range`, needs species range polygons, which the user supplies ([Custom reference points and polygons](gazetteers.html)). This article lists where each layer comes from, how the package's own reference data compare with [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s, how much the choice of land scale changes the `sea` test, and how the reference version is recorded with the flags. Installation is covered in [Get started](OccurrenceCleaner.html).

## The layers

```{r layers}
library(OccurrenceCleaner)

ri <- reference_info()
```

```{r layers-table, echo = FALSE}
wiki <- ri$layer == "institutions_wikipedia"
shown <- ri[, c("layer", "source", "version", "retrieved")]
fb <- ri$layer == "factbook"
shown$version[fb] <- substr(shown$version[fb], 1, nchar("factbook.json ") + 7)
shown$version[wiki] <- "7 page revisions (below)"
shown$source[ri$layer == "habitat"] <- "IRMNG (Rees 2026)"
shown$source[ri$layer == "aohi"] <- "AHOI (Park et al. 2023)"
shown$retrieved <- sprintf('<span style="white-space: nowrap">%s</span>',
                           shown$retrieved)
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("Layer", "Source", "Version / snapshot",
                                  "Retrieved"))
```

`reference_info()` lists each source's version, file name, download URL, SHA-256 checksum and licence.

- The factbook version is the shortened commit hash of the factbook.json mirror. `reference_info()` gives the full hash.

- Wikipedia lists use fixed page revisions: `r gsub(" revision", "", ri$version[wiki])`.

- The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera (IRMNG) is cited as: Rees, T. (compiler) (2026), *The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera*, available from [irmng.org](https://www.irmng.org) at VLIZ.

- The layer name `aohi` follows CoordinateCleaner's [`cc_aohi()`](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/reference/cc_aohi.html). The inventory itself uses the abbreviation AHOI.

The tests use the following layers:

```{r layer-use, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  test = c("capital", "centroid", "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "aohi", "sea", "urban", "country_mismatch",
           "sea_nonmarine, land_marine"),
  `reference data` = c("CIA World Factbook capital coordinates, Natural Earth populated places: admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories",
                       "CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org World Borders and GEOLocate country points, Natural Earth admin-0 polygon centroids and label points, admin-1 label points",
                       "CoordinateCleaner's institutions, 573 moved (565 to their Google Maps place), and the confirmed points of GBIF GRSciColl, Wikidata, Wikipedia's lists of natural history museums, BGCI, Index Herbariorum, the GBIF registry and OpenStreetMap",
                       "one fixed point, 12.58 E, 55.67 N",
                       "Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023), 308 points",
                       "Natural Earth land at 1:110 million (default), 1:50 million or 1:10 million",
                       "Natural Earth urban areas 1:50 million",
                       "Natural Earth admin-0 countries 1:50 million",
                       "the land of sea, and genus habitats from the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

The sections below give the provenance of each layer: its sources, their licences and retrieval dates, and how the points were matched or placed.

### Capitals

The capitals are the capital "geographic coordinates" of the CIA World Factbook, the source of [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s capitals, read from the same factbook.json mirror: one point per country profile, 232 in all. The Natural Earth admin-0 capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories (243) are added with `extension` `TRUE`.

### Country and province centroids

The country centroids come from the three sources CoordinateCleaner's table is compiled from, each taken from the source itself:

- The "Geographic coordinates" of the CIA World Factbook (public domain), read from the factbook.json mirror of the Factbook country profiles on 2026-10-11: 275 points.

- The label points of the World Borders Dataset 0.3 by Bjorn Sandvik, thematicmapping.org, under CC BY-SA, from the GeoJSON conversion of the dataset at github.com/jeffaudi/world-borders-geojson: 246 points.

- Every point the GEOLocate georeferencing service (geo-locate.org) returns when a country name is entered as country and locality, queried on 2026-10-11 for each country name of the three tables: 548 points. GEOLocate also returns places that carry a country's name. One such place, Niger State in Nigeria for "Niger", lies inside another country more than 100 km from the queried one and is left out.

The Natural Earth admin-0 polygon centroids, computed on the sphere, and label points (516) are added with `extension` `TRUE`. The province centroids are the Natural Earth admin-1 label points.

### Land, countries and urban areas

The land, country and urban-area polygons are Natural Earth layers at the scales the table above gives. All Natural Earth layers are in the public domain; the Natural Earth terms of use say that "No permission is needed to use Natural Earth."

### Institutions

The institution test uses the 9,773 institutions with coordinates in CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1's table, and the points of other sources that a check beyond their own source confirms. The `status` column of `reference_points("institution")` says which a point is: `"cc"`, `"override"`, `"confirmed"` or `"unconfirmed"`. The test leaves the unconfirmed points out.

```{r inst-status}
inst <- reference_points("institution")
table(inst$source, inst$status)
```

Of CoordinateCleaner's points, 9,200 are used as that package has them. The other 573 are moved. Of these, 565 are moved to the place Google Maps gives for the institution. For each of them, a Google Maps place with the institution's name lies within 25 km of the city in CoordinateCleaner's record, while CoordinateCleaner's point lies more than 25 km from both that place and the city. The median distance between the two points is 430 km. CoordinateCleaner places Duke University, listed in Durham, North Carolina, in southern California, for example. The SCAR Expert Group on Birds and Marine Mammals has no site of its own; it is moved from a point in France to the secretariat of SCAR, the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research, in Cambridge. Seven more, whose Google Maps search gave no place, are moved to the site Wikipedia or OpenStreetMap gives: the Canadian National Mycological Herbarium, for example, from Edmonton to the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa. The `cc_lon` and `cc_lat` columns keep CoordinateCleaner's coordinates, and `evidence` names the place and the URL its coordinates were read from.

Every one of CoordinateCleaner's points was searched in Google Maps by name, city and country between 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-23, and 630 met the conditions above. A review of each match kept 65 of them at CoordinateCleaner's coordinates:

- 42 where the Google Maps place is a different institution;

- 9 where the name is generic or the place is the town itself;

- 12 organisations with several sites where the record does not name the site;

- 1 large site, a wildlife refuge, where the Google Maps place is one point of it;

- 1 where the institution's own address confirms CoordinateCleaner's point.

For the 39 points whose Google Maps search gave no place, the site was looked up in Wikipedia, OpenStreetMap and the institutions' own pages. Of these, 26 lie within 25 km of CoordinateCleaner's point and one could not be identified. Seven are moved. Five stay at CoordinateCleaner's coordinates: an organisation with several sites, one whose site no source confirms, and three databases or networks with no site of their own.

A point from another source is confirmed when a Google Maps place with the institution's name lies within 300 m of it, or when it lies within 200 m of the OpenStreetMap feature with that name. Points taken from OpenStreetMap need the Google Maps check. These checks covered the point nearest each of CoordinateCleaner's institutions and confirm 2,786 points.

The other points come from the sources below. The first set is the bulk export of GBIF's Global Registry of Scientific Collections (GRSciColl), retrieved on 2026-10-09: 10,002 institutions, of which 6,085 have coordinates. The five of these that the `zero` test would flag are left out: four are registered within 0.14 degrees of (0, 0), although they are in Portugal, Nigeria, Turkey and Taiwan, and one has a longitude of exactly 0. Kept, they would mark every record at (0, 0) as lying at an institution as well. GRSciColl absorbed the Global Registry of Biodiversity Repositories (GRBio) in 2018 and is synchronised weekly with Index Herbariorum. GBIF publishes the registry through its open API and states no separate licence for it.

The institution table includes locations from Wikidata, Wikipedia, GeoNames and Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI). The `source` column of `reference_points("institution")` identifies the source of each point.

Wikidata (CC0, queried 2026-10-10) supplies coordinates for:

- Botanical gardens, natural history museums, zoos, public aquaria and herbaria, including items in subclasses of these categories.

- Museums whose main subject or field of work is a natural-history discipline, such as geology, paleontology, zoology or botany.

- Museums in Wikipedia's English "List of natural history museums", which supplies CoordinateCleaner's Wikipedia entries, and its Arabic, Dutch, Esperanto, French, German and Portuguese counterparts.

The Wikipedia lists contain 2,331 entries (CC BY-SA 4.0, retrieved 2026-10-11). Entries are matched to Wikidata through their linked articles. Entries without an article are matched when a single museum item in the same country has the corresponding name and lies within 25 km of the named town.

After removing duplicate Wikidata items, these sources provide 7,810 points: 3,263 botanical gardens, 1,835 museums, 2,609 zoos and aquaria, and 103 herbaria. None has zero coordinates.

Museums without their own Wikidata coordinates are located using the place named in the Wikipedia entry. This is either the Wikidata location of a linked town or university, checked against the entry's country, or a GeoNames populated place matching the named town (CC BY 4.0). This adds 700 points, including 385 from the English list. Entries without a town are omitted.

The three GeoNames locations in CoordinateCleaner's table come from the GeoNames country files (CC BY 4.0).

BGCI's [GardenSearch map](https://tools.bgci.org/map.php), retrieved for all countries on 2026-10-10, lists 3,765 gardens. Of these, 3,653 have coordinates; removing one at zero coordinates leaves 3,652 points. These are used under the [BGCI terms](https://www.bgci.org/terms-and-conditions/).

Two further registries were downloaded in full on 2026-10-13:

- Index Herbariorum, the New York Botanical Garden's herbarium registry, provides locations for 4,805 herbaria. The table adds the 1,062 for which GRSciColl lacks coordinates under the same herbarium code.

- The GBIF registry provides coordinates for 2,468 of its 3,639 publishing organisations. All 2,468 are added.

The remaining institutions with coordinates in CoordinateCleaner's table are located using their name, city and country. An institution is already represented if an entry matches its name, its full Index Herbariorum name, or an alternative or collection name recorded by GRSciColl.

Each remaining institution is looked up in this order:

1. Wikidata, using its full name or the part before the first comma.

2. OpenStreetMap through Nominatim, accepting a result that matches at least half the institution's name words or lies within 25 km of CoordinateCleaner's point.

3. GeoNames, using the city listed by CoordinateCleaner or GRSciColl.

When several candidates are returned, the candidate nearest CoordinateCleaner's point is selected. Coordinates come from the selected source.

If these searches find no location, the institution is considered represented when an existing point lies within 25 km and matches at least 60% of its name words. Otherwise, it is assigned to the populated place mentioned in its name or, as a last resort, the populated place in its country nearest CoordinateCleaner's point. These entries have `source = "CoordinateCleaner list"`; `master_source` records how they were located.

A last step checks the location of every institution of CoordinateCleaner's table against OpenStreetMap. The named OpenStreetMap features of institution kinds (universities, colleges, research institutes and offices, museums, zoos, aquaria and botanical gardens) were retrieved on 2026-10-13 from the Overpass API: 258,691 features. A feature is the institution when every distinctive word of one of its names occurs in the institution's name, those words cover at least half of the institution's own distinctive words, and the feature lies within 25 km of CoordinateCleaner's point. This finds a feature for 4,818 institutions. Where CoordinateCleaner's point lies closer to the feature than every point of this table that stands for the institution, the feature's point is added with `master_source = "OpenStreetMap feature of that name"`. This adds 1,134 points. OpenStreetMap data are © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database Licence.

### Genus habitats

The habitat tests `sea_nonmarine` and `land_marine` use genus classifications from the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera (IRMNG), supplied as a Darwin Core archive dated 2026-10-06 under CC BY 4.0. IRMNG records marine, brackish, freshwater and terrestrial flags for each name. Following the rule in `reference_habitat()`, the package classifies 296,474 genera as nonmarine and 21,891 as exclusively marine, with kingdom used to distinguish names.

The citation is: Rees, T. (compiler) (2026). *The Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera*. Available from [irmng.org](https://www.irmng.org) at VLIZ.

### Artificial hotspots

The Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (AHOI; [Park, Xie, Thammavong, Tulaiha and Feng, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1111/jbi.14543)) identifies coordinates that recur most often in GBIF records and records why they recur. The authors' [Dryad deposit](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.v41ns1s0p), released under CC0, supplies 308 points with coordinates: 154 for plants, 51 for birds, 51 for insects and 52 for mammals.

CoordinateCleaner's bundled `aohi` table contains 309 points. The two datasets share 303 points; differences involve a few bird locations and one plant latitude, recorded as 42.26° N in CoordinateCleaner and 42.20° N in the deposit.

Scripts in the source repository's `data-raw/` directory rebuild the layers from their source datasets.

## How the reference data differ from CoordinateCleaner's

The package's reference points describe the same places as [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) 3.0.1's `countryref` and `institutions` tables, but they are not the same tables. Counts as of 2026-10-17, the date of the last institution check:

```{r compare, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  gazetteer = c("capitals", "country centroids", "province centroids", "institutions"),
  CoordinateCleaner = c("225 (one per ISO3 code)", "660 rows from the CIA World Factbook, thematicmapping.org and GEOLocate",
                        "4,645 (older Natural Earth admin-1 label points)",
                        "9,773 with coordinates (GRBio, Index Herbariorum, GBIF, BGCI, Wikipedia, GeoNames)"),
  OccurrenceCleaner = c("475: 232 Factbook capitals and 243 Natural Earth capitals, alternative capitals and dependent-territory capitals marked as extension",
                        "1,585: 1,069 from the same three sources (275 Factbook, 246 World Borders, 548 GEOLocate) and 516 Natural Earth polygon centroids and label points marked as extension",
                        "4,594 (Natural Earth 5.1.1 admin-1 label points)",
                        "12,559 used by the test: CoordinateCleaner's 9,773 (573 moved, 565 of them to their Google Maps place) and 2,786 confirmed points of other sources; 22,133 unconfirmed points left out")))
```

- **Capitals.** Of CoordinateCleaner's 225 capital points, 221 match this package's Factbook points when rounded to 0.01 degrees. Rounding shifts their positions by up to 523 m. The remaining four reflect Factbook entries that have since changed: Bujumbura to Gitega for Burundi; Buenos Aires from 58°40′ W to 58°22′ W, correcting a location 27 km west of the city; Melekeok to Ngerulmud for Palau; and a 1.8 km coordinate adjustment for Rangoon.

  Natural Earth adds alternative and official capitals, including Cape Town and Bloemfontein alongside Pretoria, Sucre alongside La Paz, Naypyidaw alongside Yangon, and Dodoma alongside Dar es Salaam. Selecting `extension = FALSE` excludes these additions.

- **Country centroids.** Of CoordinateCleaner's 660 points, 645 match this package's points exactly. India, Italy and the United Kingdom use World Borders coordinates that changed in version 0.3. GEOLocate no longer returns three points for Macedonia or a point for Guinea located at sea at 10° W, 5° N. The remaining eight points lie between 5 m and 68 km from the nearest point in this package.

  Natural Earth adds polygon centres, which lie a median of 30 km from CoordinateCleaner's centroids and flag records georeferenced to those centres. Selecting `extension = FALSE` excludes these additions.

- **Province centroids.** CoordinateCleaner uses Natural Earth administrative label points: 4,566 of its 4,645 rows match codes and coordinates in releases 3.3.0, 4.0.0 or 4.1.0. This package uses release 5.1.1. All province points therefore carry `extension = FALSE`, since they come from the same source.

  Of CoordinateCleaner's rows, 4,591 match this package's points exactly. Of the remaining 54, 50 lie more than 10 km from any included point: 15 use coordinates Natural Earth has since changed, and 39 match no tagged release.

- **Institutions.** The institution test uses CoordinateCleaner's 9,773 institution points, 9,200 of them at CoordinateCleaner's coordinates and 573 moved, 565 of them to the Google Maps place of the institution ([Institutions](#institutions) gives the conditions). It also uses 2,786 points of other sources that a check has confirmed. A record near a moved or confirmed point is flagged here and not by CoordinateCleaner.

  CoordinateCleaner geocoded nearly all its institutions itself. For example, it located 641 of its 712 BGCI gardens from names and addresses, while this package's BGCI points have BGCI's coordinates. A confirmed point can therefore mark another building of an institution than CoordinateCleaner's point. `reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` uses CoordinateCleaner's table as it is.

The following example shows how the capital references affect flags for records at alternative or official capitals:

```{r capitals, eval = has_cc, message = FALSE}
x <- data.frame(city = c("Pretoria", "Cape Town", "La Paz", "Sucre", "Yangon", "Naypyidaw"),
                species = "a",
                decimalLongitude = c(28.19, 18.42, -68.15, -65.26, 96.16, 96.13),
                decimalLatitude = c(-25.75, -33.92, -16.50, -19.04, 16.80, 19.75))
data.frame(city = x$city,
           OccurrenceCleaner = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital,
           CoordinateCleaner = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital)
```

Cape Town, Sucre and Naypyidaw are flagged only through the Natural Earth extension points; Pretoria, La Paz and Yangon under both. Which list is right depends on what an error looks like: a herbarium sheet in Cape Town georeferenced to the city is as wrong under either reference, and only the extension points catch it.

## Extension points

The capital, country centroid and institution tables also contain points from sources CoordinateCleaner does not use, marked `extension` `TRUE`:

- capitals: 243 Natural Earth capitals, alternative capitals and capitals of dependent territories;

- country centroids: 516 Natural Earth polygon centroids and label points;

- institutions: 7,660 points, the botanical gardens, natural history museums, zoos, aquaria and herbaria of Wikidata beyond the museums of the English Wikipedia list, and the museums of the Arabic, Dutch, Esperanto, French, German and Portuguese lists. No check has confirmed any of them, so the institution test leaves them out.

The capital and centroid tests use them by default. Passing the rows with `extension` `FALSE` through `gazetteers` restricts a test to CoordinateCleaner's sources; for the capitals above, that leaves Cape Town, Sucre and Naypyidaw unflagged:

```{r extension, eval = has_cc}
g <- reference_points("capital")
data.frame(city = x$city,
           all = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital,
           cc_sources = flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital",
                                         gazetteers = list(capital = g[!g$extension, ]))$flag_capital)
```

## Land scale and the `sea` test

The `sea` test flags records outside the land polygons. It supports Natural Earth land polygons at scales of 1:110 million, 1:50 million and 1:10 million. OccurrenceCleaner defaults to 1:110 million (`land_scale = 110`). [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) defaults to 1:110 million in `cc_sea()` and 1:50 million in `clean_coordinates()`. The 1:10 million layer is downloaded on first use and cached.

The coarse 1:110 million layer smooths the coast and drops small islands; the 1:50 million layer follows the coast more closely. A grid of points over Denmark and the western Baltic shows where the two disagree:

```{r land-grid}
g <- expand.grid(decimalLongitude = seq(7.5, 15.5, by = 0.05),
                 decimalLatitude = seq(54, 58, by = 0.05))
g$species <- "a"
s110 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea")$flag_sea
s50 <- flag_occurrences(g, tests = "sea", land_scale = 50)$flag_sea
g$verdict <- ifelse(s110 & s50, "sea at both", ifelse(!s110 & !s50, "land at both",
                    ifelse(s110, "sea at 1:110 million only", "sea at 1:50 million only")))
table(g$verdict)
```

```{r land-map, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 5}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(g, aes(decimalLongitude, decimalLatitude, fill = verdict)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`land at both` = "#C8B88A", `sea at both` = "#A9C7E0",
                               `sea at 1:110 million only` = "#C0392B", `sea at 1:50 million only` = "#2C3E50")) +
  coord_quickmap(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "longitude", y = "latitude", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical") +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))
```

```{r land-share, include = FALSE}
dis <- mean(s110 != s50)
```

On this grid the two scales disagree for `r round(100 * dis, 1)` % of the points, all of them along the coast. At 1:110 million Funen, Lolland, Falster, Rügen and Bornholm are missing, so records on them are flagged as at sea (red); the coarse 1:110 million coastline also reaches out into the water, so records in a strip of coastal water count as on land there and are flagged only at 1:50 million (dark). For coastal and island taxa the scale therefore changes a share of the `sea` flags large enough to see in a tally. The 1:10 million layer is the most detailed of the three:

```{r land-10, eval = FALSE}
download_reference("land_10")
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "sea", land_scale = 10)
```

The download is checked against the SHA-256 in `reference_info()` and refused if Natural Earth has published a different file under the same name. The converted layer is stored in `tools::R_user_dir("OccurrenceCleaner", "cache")`, so it is downloaded once per machine.

## Buffers

The buffers are the other half of every proximity test. They default to [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s (10 km for capitals, 1 km for centroids and the GBIF headquarters, 100 m for institutions, 0.5 degrees around (0, 0)) and are changed per test:

```{r buffers}
x <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(16.37, 16.45), decimalLatitude = c(48.21, 48.21))
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital")$flag_capital
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "capital", buffers = list(capital = 2000))$flag_capital
```

A buffer of 2 km for capitals keeps records from the outer districts of a capital while still removing those placed at the city's coordinates. The 0.5-degree zero buffer is in degrees, the others in metres.

## Recording the reference

Every flagged data frame carries the reference that produced it, with the version of each layer. The printed object shows the short form; `flag_reference()` returns the full label, which names every layer with its version, snapshot date or page revision:

```{r stamp}
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("capital", "sea"), land_scale = 50)
f
attr(f, "occ_layout_version")
```

```{r stamp-label}
flag_reference(f)
```

`reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` stamps the installed [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) version instead. For streamed input the same label is written to the output directory, and a rerun into that directory with a different reference, land scale, set of tests or layout stops with an error, so one output directory never mixes flags from two references.

## Choosing a reference

- `reference = "OccurrenceCleaner"` (the default) needs no other package, has a version and checksum for every layer, and uses current Natural Earth, GRSciColl, Wikidata, Wikipedia, GeoNames, BGCI, Index Herbariorum, GBIF registry and OpenStreetMap data.

- Set `reference = "CoordinateCleaner"` to use [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s own reference tables, for example to compare with a published analysis that used it. This requires CoordinateCleaner to be installed and reproduces its flags subject to the differences documented in [Compatibility with CoordinateCleaner](coordinatecleaner.html). The polygon tests also need [rnaturalearth](https://docs.ropensci.org/rnaturalearth/), which downloads the Natural Earth layers at run time as CoordinateCleaner does.

Both references use the same buffers and the same geodesic distance, so the difference between them is in the points and polygons only.
